newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Supreme Court hears English-only arguments.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Supreme Court hears English-only arguments.

text.p: The U.S. Supreme Court made clear on Wednesday that technical problems with the case would prevent it from reaching the merits of a free-speech challenge to a state law requiring government workers speak only English.

The justices during the hour-long arguments strongly suggested the case would have to be dismissed, partly because the state of Arizona early in the legal battle decided not to enforce the controversial measure.

"Why didn't this case end? Wasn't it moot at that point?" Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg asked an attorney for a group called Arizonans for Official English, which pursued the case after the state decided against appealing.

All the questioning centred on technical or procedural legal points of whether the case was moot or judicially irrelevant, and jurisdiction. The justices did not address the free-speech constitutional issues.

Arizona voters in 1988 barely approved an initiative barring the use of any language other than English by state workers in their official duties. It was the most restrictive of the English-only laws adopted by about half of the states.

The Arizona law was immediately challenged in court by Maria-Kelley Yniguez, an employee of the department of administration who handled medical malpractice claims. She was fluent in both English and Spanish, and feared she would be disciplined under the law.
A federal judge and a U.S. appeals court declared the law violated her constitutional free-speech rights.

But Justice Sandra Day O'Connor asked why the case did not become moot when Yniguez left her state job in 1990. She also questioned if the English-only group had legal standing to pursue the appeal in place of the state.
Justice Anthony Kennedy said to Barnaby Zall, the group's lawyer, "All your organisation did was put something on the ballot." He later added, "It seems to me there is no controversy here."
Justice Antonin Scalia expressed a similar view, saying "He wants to have the case here, but I don't see how it is here." He asked Zall what the Supreme Court should rule.
Zall replied he would prefer for the case to be decided on the merits, but that if the case was moot the justices should set aside the appeals court and the judge's rulings.
Robert Pohlman, an attorney representing Yniguez, did not fare much better.
Kennedy asked whether the governor or state attorney general ever threatened to discipline Yniguez or other state employees for speaking Spanish at work.
"There was no specific indication," Pohlman admitted, but he claimed the law had "a chilling effect" on her free-speech rights.
But Justice David Souter asked how her rights could have been threatened when the governor had gone on record as saying workers could use Spanish if needed.
The justices took the case under advisement, with a ruling due later in its 1996-97 term.
